details:
SPHEREx WhyLab is an interactive astronomy platform developed by Team NovaScale to help users explore real NASA SPHEREx observations, compare images and investigate possible changes in the sky.

Users begin by selecting a target and opening its observations. The application includes 21 real FITS files across five targets: Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis. Each observation retains information such as its date, detector, source catalogue and supplied position estimates. Selected observations can be processed into aligned previews and compared in a sequence.

WhyLab also supports exploratory motion testing. Users separate suitable observations into training and independent reserved exposures, then examine whether the results support possible motion. The application reports insufficient evidence when the data cannot support a reliable conclusion. Users can export their investigation evidence for review.

The project makes astronomical data more approachable for students and astronomy enthusiasts. It connects visual exploration with scientific questioning, encouraging users to ask what caused a change rather than assuming that every difference represents a discovery. Interactive 3D illustrations and space games provide an additional educational experience, separate from the scientific analysis.

The backend uses Python, FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib and Pillow. The frontend uses JavaScript, React and Vite, with Aladin Lite for sky navigation and Three.js for 3D visualizations. Docker packages the application, GitHub hosts the source code and Render hosts the public demonstration.

A key design choice is to load downloaded observations first. This keeps the core workflow available when IRSA cannot be reached. Optional background checks can reconcile matching archive records and add observations when available. The sky explorer also includes a bundled reference overview.

During development, Team NovaScale considered data provenance, observation epochs, image quality, wavelength differences, limited hosting resources and external-service reliability. The current application is a prototype: saved investigations are temporary, and important evidence should be exported. Coverage, a bright pixel or a supplied target association does not independently confirm an astronomical detection or discovery.
